turns.prompt_text: I now have a bunch of these metal plates from this microwave I took apart. is there any way I can repurpose them? can I cut them into other metal plates? I have a large volume of space
turns.response_html:
Taking apart a microwave yields some surprisingly high-quality galvanized or powder-coated steel. Since you have a large volume of space to work with, these plates are excellent for structural or organizational projects where you need something more durable than plastic or wood.

Cutting and Shaping

To answer your first question: Yes, you can absolutely cut them. Most microwave casings are made of mild steel (usually between 22 and 18 gauge).

  • Tin Snips/Aviation Snips: Good for thin gauge material and detail work, though it can slightly warp the edges.
  • Angle Grinder: Use a thin cutoff wheel for straight, clean lines. This is the fastest method for bulk plates.
  • Nibbler: If you have a drill attachment or a standalone power nibbler, this is perfect for cutting shapes without distorting the metal.
  • Safety Note: Microwave plates often have sharp, stamped edges. Always de-burr the edges with a file or sandpaper after cutting to prevent deep cuts.

Repurposing Ideas

Given your interest in hardware and 3D printing, here are a few ways to put that steel to work:

  • Custom Tool Pegboards: If the plates are large enough, you can drill a grid of holes to create custom-sized pegboards for your workshop area. Steel is much more durable than the standard fiberboard versions.
  • Magnetic Project Boards: Because these are steel, they are ferromagnetic. You can mount them to a wall or the side of a workbench to hold magnetic parts trays, hex keys, or even 3D printer nozzles.
  • Soldering/Welding Heat Shields: Use a plate as a portable "safe zone" on your workbench for soldering or using a heat gun. It protects your primary work surface from burns and solder drips.
  • 3D Printer Enclosure Panels: If you are building a custom enclosure for printing ABS or ASA, these metal plates can act as fire-resistant side panels or a base to help retain heat.
  • Component Mounting Plates: In a "large volume of space," you can use these as chassis plates for mounting heavy transformers, power supplies, or microcontrollers (like a Raspberry Pi) for stationary projects.
  • Brackets and Gussets: You can bend these plates in a vise to create "L" or "U" brackets to reinforce wooden shelving or to mount hardware to walls.

A Quick Warning

If the plates came from the internal cavity of the microwave, they are likely coated in a food-safe ceramic or powder coating. If you plan on welding them, grind off the coating first. Fumes from heated coatings or galvanized zinc can be toxic.

Since you've already dismantled the unit, did you manage to save the transformer or the magnets from the magnetron as well?

Those are the "crown jewels" of a microwave teardown. Given your interest in mechanical systems and hardware scavenging, those components open up some heavy-duty project possibilities.

The Microwave Oven Transformer (MOT)

The MOT is a beast of a component. It’s designed to step up standard wall voltage to about $2,000V+$, which makes it incredibly dangerous in its original state, but a goldmine for modification.

  • Spot Welder: This is the most popular use for a MOT. By knocking out the thin secondary high-voltage windings and replacing them with a few turns of very thick, insulated copper cable, you convert it into a high-current, low-voltage transformer. It’s perfect for welding those metal plates you just cut or for building battery packs.
  • Arc Starter: If you ever venture into TIG welding or specialized plasma projects, the core of a MOT can be repurposed as a high-frequency arc starter.
  • Heavy-Duty Power Supply: You can rewind the secondary to output specific voltages (like $12V$ or $24V$) at extremely high amperage for bench testing high-power motors or actuators.

The Magnetron Magnets

The magnets found inside the magnetron are usually high-grade ferrite "donuts." They aren't as strong as Neodymium (rare earth) magnets, but they are much more heat-resistant and durable.

  • Magnetic Tool Rail: Since you have metal plates, you can epoxy these magnets to the back of a plate and mount it to your wall. It creates a dedicated spot for heavy wrenches or pliers that won't budge.
  • Fluid Filtration: If you're doing any mechanical work (like on your Chevy Malibu), placing one of these on the outside of an oil filter or a transmission pan can help trap fine metallic shavings that the internal filter might miss.
  • Levitation/Physics Models: Because of their shape and consistent field, they are great for demonstrating eddy currents or building simple "magnetic bearing" prototypes.

A Crucial Safety Reminder

Since you have the magnetron, be extremely careful with the ceramic insulators (usually pink or white) at the tips. Some older models contain Beryllium Oxide (BeO).

Important: As long as the ceramic is intact, it is safe. Never crush, sand, or break the ceramic insulators. Inhaling the dust from Beryllium Oxide is highly toxic and can cause permanent lung damage.
